blocks.text: A hot steel billet 100 mm across is squeezed between flat dies into a pancake, and a press rated for a few meganewtons suddenly stalls. The billet looks easy to squash, yet the press needed far more force than the metal's strength alone suggests, because friction at the die faces has to be overcome too.

blocks.markdown: In **open-die upset forging** a cylinder of initial height $h_0$ is compressed between flat platens to a height $h$. The metal is incompressible, so volume is conserved: $\pi r_0^2h_0=\pi r^2h$, and the radius grows as the height falls. The material resists flow with its **flow stress** $Y_f$ (MPa), the stress needed to keep deforming it at the current strain, strain rate and temperature. Without friction the force would simply be $Y_f$ times the current cross-sectional area. With friction at the die faces the metal near the faces cannot spread freely, so the average pressure rises above $Y_f$.

blocks.title: Flow stress and friction hill
blocks.text: The flow stress $Y_f$ is the instantaneous stress at which the metal yields plastically under the actual forming conditions; for hot work it is lower and depends on strain rate. Friction between die and work makes the pressure peak at the centre of the billet face, a distribution called the friction hill, so the average die pressure exceeds $Y_f$.

blocks.latex: p_{av}\approx Y_f\left(1+\frac{2\mu r}{3h}\right), \qquad F = p_{av}\,\pi r^{2}
blocks.caption: Upset forging force; $\mu$ is the Coulomb friction coefficient, $r$ and $h$ the current radius and height. Valid for sliding friction and moderate $\mu r/h$

blocks.title: Upsetting force with friction
blocks.prompt: A cylindrical steel billet is upset to a current radius $r=50$ mm and height $h=20$ mm. The flow stress is $Y_f=300$ MPa and the friction coefficient is $\mu=0.2$. Find the average die pressure and the forging force.

steps.text: Contact area and force (MPa times mm$^2$ gives N).

blocks.answer: The average pressure is 400 MPa and the forging force is about 3.14 MN; frictionless, it would be only 2.36 MN.

blocks.markdown: Notice how the friction term grows as the billet is squashed thinner: $r$ increases and $h$ decreases, so $\mu r/h$ rises sharply near the end of the stroke. That is why the last millimetres of an upset need the largest force, and why a press must be sized for the end of the stroke, not the beginning. Lubricants (graphite, glass) cut $\mu$ and therefore the force.

**Rolling** squeezes a strip from thickness $h_0$ to $h_f$ between rotating rolls of radius $R$. The rolls pull the strip into the gap by friction. Contact starts where the roll surface meets the strip at an angle $\theta$ from the vertical, and the roll can bite only if the friction coefficient $\mu$ is at least $\tan\theta$. Using the usual small-angle geometry, contact length $L\approx\sqrt{R\,\Delta h}$ with draft $\Delta h=h_0-h_f$, and this limit gives the widely used estimate below.

blocks.caption: Maximum draft in one rolling pass; $\mu$ roll-strip friction coefficient, $R$ roll radius (same length units as $\Delta h$)

blocks.title: Maximum single-pass draft
blocks.prompt: A 12 mm thick strip is hot rolled between rolls of radius $R=250$ mm with $\mu=0.12$. Find the maximum draft, the exit thickness and the reduction.

steps.text: Reduction as a fraction of entry thickness.

blocks.answer: The strip can be reduced at most 3.6 mm in one pass (to 8.4 mm, a 30 percent reduction); a larger reduction needs a second pass, bigger rolls or higher friction.

rows: Equiaxed or columnar dendrites, random direction
blocks.caption: Typical comparison of forged and cast microstructure

blocks.title: Why forging beats casting for critical parts
blocks.text: Forging breaks down the coarse dendritic as-cast structure, closes internal voids and aligns grain flow with the part contour (for example around a crankshaft web), so strength, toughness and fatigue life are higher, particularly along the grain direction. The price is higher tooling cost and less complex shape freedom.

blocks.title: Limits of these estimates
blocks.text: The upset formula assumes Coulomb sliding friction and ignores barrelling and die chilling; for sticking friction (high $\mu r/h$) the model overestimates. The rolling limit $\mu^2R$ is a bite estimate for a single pass; actual passes are usually well below it.

points: Upset forging force is $F=p_{av}\pi r^2$ with $p_{av}\approx Y_f(1+2\mu r/3h)$; friction raises force, and it rises steeply as the billet flattens.
Volume constancy gives the radius at each stage: $r=r_0\sqrt{h_0/h}$.
The largest single-pass draft in rolling is about $\mu^2R$, so bigger rolls or rougher (higher-friction) rolls allow heavier reductions.
Forging refines grain, closes porosity and aligns grain flow, giving better fatigue and impact properties than as-cast metal.

questions.stem: A cylinder is upset between flat dies. Which change will increase the forging force at a given height and flow stress?

options.text: Using a graphite lubricant
Increasing the friction coefficient at the die faces
Reducing the billet radius at that stage
Lowering the contact friction by polishing the dies

questions.correctOptionText: Increasing the friction coefficient at the die faces

distractorRationale.a: Lubrication lowers $\mu$, so the friction term in the pressure falls and the force drops.
distractorRationale.c: A smaller radius reduces area and the friction term $2\mu r/3h$, both lowering force.
distractorRationale.d: Polishing reduces friction, which reduces force.

questions.explanation: The average pressure is $Y_f(1+2\mu r/3h)$, so increasing $\mu$ directly increases the die pressure and the force. The other options all lower friction or area.

questions.stem: A steel cylinder is upset between flat dies. At a given instant the radius is 25 mm and the height is 10 mm. Take flow stress 250 MPa and friction coefficient 0.15. Calculate the forging force in kN using $p_{av}=Y_f(1+2\mu r/3h)$.

A cylindrical billet of diameter 40 mm and height 60 mm is upset to a height of 15 mm. At the end of the stroke the flow stress is 400 MPa and the friction coefficient is 0.1. Using volume constancy and $p_{av}=Y_f(1+2\mu r/3h)$, calculate the final forging force in MN.
questions.explanation: Volume constancy gives $r=20\sqrt{60/15}=40$ mm. Then $p_{av}=400(1+2(0.1)(40)/(3\times15))=471.1$ MPa and $A=\pi(40)^2=5027$ mm$^2$, so $F=2.37$ MN.

questions.stem: Which expression estimates the maximum draft (thickness reduction) in a single rolling pass with roll radius $R$ and friction coefficient $\mu$?

options.text: $\Delta h_{max}\approx\mu R$
$\Delta h_{max}\approx R/\mu$
$\Delta h_{max}\approx\mu^{2}/R$
$\Delta h_{max}\approx\mu^{2}R$

distractorRationale.a: A linear dependence on $\mu$ would not match the bite geometry, where draft goes with $\tan^2$ of the contact angle.
distractorRationale.b: This would make the draft fall as friction rises, which is the opposite of what happens: friction pulls the strip in.
distractorRationale.c: This has the wrong dimensions (not a length) and makes draft fall with roll radius.

questions.explanation: The bite condition $\mu\ge\tan\theta$ with contact length $L=\sqrt{R\Delta h}\approx R\tan\theta$ gives $\Delta h_{max}\approx\mu^2R$. The draft therefore rises with the square of friction and in direct proportion to roll radius.

questions.stem: Cold rolling is carried out with rolls of radius 400 mm and a friction coefficient of 0.08. Estimate the maximum draft in a single pass, in mm, using $\Delta h_{max}=\mu^2R$.
questions.explanation: Substituting gives $\Delta h_{max}=(0.08)^2(400)=2.56$ mm. Cold rolling with good lubrication has a small $\mu$, so the possible draft per pass is small and many passes are needed.

questions.stem: A mill wants a larger reduction per pass on the same strip without changing the rolling temperature. Which action helps most, using the bite condition?

options.text: Use larger-diameter rolls
Apply a heavier lubricant film to the rolls
Reduce the roll radius
Use polished rolls

distractorRationale.b: Lower friction lowers the bite limit; the rolls would slip rather than draw the strip in.
distractorRationale.c: A smaller radius reduces the maximum draft in proportion to $R$.
distractorRationale.d: Polishing lowers friction, so it also lowers the maximum draft.

questions.explanation: Since $\Delta h_{max}\approx\mu^2R$, increasing $R$ allows a bigger bite for the same friction coefficient. Lubricating or polishing lowers $\mu$, and a lower $\mu$ lowers the limit quadratically.

questions.stem: Compared with an as-cast structure of the same alloy, what is the typical microstructural effect of forging?

options.text: Grain size becomes larger and more random
Porosity increases because the metal is stretched
Coarse dendrites are broken down, porosity closes and grain flow follows the part shape
Grain flow becomes completely isotropic and shape-independent

questions.correctOptionText: Coarse dendrites are broken down, porosity closes and grain flow follows the part shape

distractorRationale.a: Deformation and recrystallisation refine the grain rather than coarsen it.
distractorRationale.b: Compressive forging squeezes voids shut; it does not create them.
distractorRationale.d: Forging deliberately produces directional grain flow that follows the part, which is why it gives anisotropic strength.

questions.explanation: Forging breaks down the as-cast dendritic structure, welds shut shrinkage voids and aligns the grain with the shape. This is why forged parts usually have better toughness and fatigue strength than cast ones.

questions.stem: A forged crankshaft is generally preferred to a cast crankshaft for a high-performance engine. Which reason is most directly linked to grain structure?

options.text: Forged shafts are free of any surface roughness
Casting cannot produce a part with a circular cross-section
Forged parts are always cheaper to tool
Grain flow follows the crank-web contours, so fatigue cracks must cross grains

questions.correctOptionText: Grain flow follows the crank-web contours, so fatigue cracks must cross grains

distractorRationale.a: Surface finish is a separate matter and many forgings need machining.
distractorRationale.b: Casting readily produces round sections; this is not the limitation.
distractorRationale.c: Forging dies are expensive, so cost is not the grain-structure argument.

questions.explanation: Aligned grain flow means that crack paths must run across the grain boundaries rather than along them, improving fatigue life where stresses are highest. Cast parts have randomly oriented grains and possible porosity that act as crack starters.

questions.stem: A student upsets a lubricated and an unlubricated aluminium billet, both from 50 mm to 15 mm high, and finds the unlubricated one needs a much larger force and barrels badly. Explain using the friction hill idea and the upset force relation why the force differs and why the difference grows as the billet flattens.
markingGuide: Friction at the die faces restrains radial flow near the faces
Pressure is highest at the centre (friction hill), raising the average pressure above $Y_f$
$p_{av}=Y_f(1+2\mu r/3h)$ with larger $\mu$ for the unlubricated billet
As $h$ decreases and $r$ increases, $\mu r/h$ grows so the friction term grows
Notes lubrication reduces force and barrelling, or the die contact area rise
questions.explanation: Friction resists outward metal flow and builds up a pressure hill. Because the friction term scales with $r/h$, both a higher $\mu$ and a flatter billet increase the average pressure and hence the force.

questions.stem: Explain (a) why the roll cannot pull a strip in once the reduction exceeds a certain limit, and what changes the limit, and (b) why hot rolling a cast ingot into plate improves its mechanical properties.
markingGuide: (a) The rolls pull the strip in by friction; bite requires $\mu\ge\tan\theta$ where $\theta$ is the contact angle
Larger draft means a larger contact angle; beyond $\Delta h\approx\mu^2R$ the rolls slip
Limit is increased by larger roll radius or higher friction (rougher rolls, no lubricant at the entry)
(b) Hot working breaks down coarse dendritic cast structure and closes porosity
Recrystallisation refines grains and the structure becomes elongated and more uniform, improving strength, toughness and ductility
questions.explanation: The bite condition ties the maximum draft to $\mu^2R$, so a bigger roll or more friction increases it. Hot rolling replaces coarse cast dendrites with finer recrystallised grain and welds up voids, raising properties.
